newsitem.title: ALBANIA: New Albanian standoff blocks cabinet formation.
newsitem.headline: New Albanian standoff blocks cabinet formation.

text.p: A standoff between Albanian President Sali Berisha and the new parliamentary majority is blocking the formation of a government almost three weeks after the first round of voting.

Electoral commission officials said the results were ready, but seven of the commission's 17 members were refusing to sign them because they wanted guarantees that Berisha would leave office as promised after convening the new parliament.

Diplomats who have urged a new government to get to work say they are concerned that there may be no prime minister to attend a donors' meeting in Rome at the end of July to discuss aid for the shattered country.

"Yesterday it became finally clear that Berisha will leave his post after he has appointed for the winners of June 29 a prime minister who would not govern the country but would be to his liking," Koha Jone daily said in an editorial.

"It seems we should wait once again for the people of (the southern town) of Vlore to come out in force in Flag Square, this time to remove physically from the presidency the man who took Albania into an undeclared war."

Vlore was the flashpoint of largely spontaneous demonstrations by citizens who lost their savings in the collapse of fraudulent investment schemes. The protests degenerated into battles between rival gangs.
With all but two results declared, the reformed ex-communist Socialists and their coalition allies have 115 seats in the 153-seat assembly. Berisha's Democratic Party suffered a resounding defeat.
Berisha reiterated on Thursday that he was ready to step down and blamed the Socialists for holding up the process.

He accused his opponents of whipping up a climate of terror to help them win the elections, but said he recognised the Socialists' triumph and wanted to convene the new parliament as soon as possible.
"The Socialists are showing they do not have the necessary qualities to make their start as a ruling party," said Albania daily, which is close to Berisha's Democratic Party.
"Infected by the Berisha fear virus, they are trying to begin a life in government not by fulfilling the promises they have given to the people but by eliminating their opponents."
Berisha's government, elected in disputed polls last year, resigned in March at the height of the protests triggered by the collapse of get-rich-quick pyramid schemes.

Accusations by the Socialists that Berisha was behind the delay in convening the new parliament followed suggestions by Berisha's supporters that Socialist leader Fatos Nano might be ineligible for the prime minister's post because of a conviction for embezzlement.
His supporters say the charges were politically motivated and he was pardoned by Berisha earlier this year.

Divisions are also reported in Berisha's Democrats over whether the party should rally behind the president or distance itself from him and find a new leader to improve its image, and the party is threatening to boycott the first session of parliament.

On Thursday European envoy to Albania Franz Vranitzky warned politicians to get to work or risk being abandoned by the international community, and expressed concern that the withdrawal of international peacekeepers which began this week could leave a security vacuum.

"I want to state clearly that the winners and losers of the election have to stand up to their democratic responsibilities. Should this not happen, should they return to their old games, the international community will not be willing to cooperate," he said in Vienna.
